transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (GreenCart ML), Tom Nguyen (GreenCart Infra), Sarah Lee (GreenCart Product), David Park (Data Eng)

Summary (auto): Quick review of last week's run; cost numbers updated; caching produced ~20-30% savings; need a full 100k request benchmark; next steps to share configs and updated spreadsheet.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for joining, hope folks can hear me ok
[00:05] Priya: yeah loud and clear, thanks, quick heads up we'll be on a timebox today, Tom has a 3:45, so we'll try to keep to 45
[00:12] Lena: perfect. Marco and I will go through the numbers we collected from the pilot last 48 hours and then go into caching and batching tradeoffs.
[00:21] Marco: FYI some of the logs have the model name spelled weird; the transcriber shows 7-B as 7 dash B, ignore that, real model is redwood-7b-qa quantized.
[00:30] Tom: noted, thanks.
[00:33] Marco: ok first slide, throughput. With the current Dedicated node config (1 x p4-equivalent) and our batching at avg batch size 6, we measured median throughput ~420 tokens/sec per node, p95 around 380. Cost for that node is $2.80/hr in the pilot pricing we used.
[00:50] Sarah: can you translate that into tokens per dollar? that's the number our finance team cares about.
[00:55] Marco: sure. If you take 420 tokens/sec and divide by $2.80, you get roughly 150 tokens/sec per dollar. Over an hour that is about 540k tokens per dollar-hour, approximately. There's some fuzziness because of short-tail bursts and idle time.
[01:15] Priya: ok so 150 tokens/sec/$, is that with or without caching?
[01:20] Marco: that's raw generation. With prefix/KV cache enabled for repeated prompts we saw effective tokens generated drop about 28% on the sample workload - so cost per effective token went down roughly the same percent, all else equal.
[01:33] David: how do you count "effective tokens"? is that tokens generated by model or tokens after cache hop?
[01:38] Marco: good q — effective tokens here means tokens actually emitted by the model. If a request hits the cache for the first N tokens, those don't incur generation CPU/GPU. So your billable generation decreases. Our numbers are based on model-side generation tokens.
[01:52] Tom: in our traffic maybe 40% of calls are repeat product descriptions so cache hit could be higher with smarter keys.
[01:58] Marco: exactly, and in those cases you get multiplicative savings. On the flip side caching adds complexity for invalidation and cold-starts.
[02:08] Lena: quick interjection: Priya had asked last week about batch sizing impact on latency — can you run that through?
[02:13] Marco: yes. We ran batch sizes 1, 4, 8. At batch 1 median latency (end-to-end) was ~120ms per request, at batch 4 it rose to 180ms median but throughput improved; batch 8 gives best throughput ~620 tokens/sec but p95 latency spikes to 700-900ms for small requests. For web interactions Sarah described, p95 matters more.
[02:32] Sarah: right, if we have chat-like UX we need p95 under 300ms ideally. Those 700ms tails would be noticeable.
[02:38] Marco: tradeoff is you lose unit economics when you force small batches; but we can use dynamic batching — send small requests immediately, coalesce only when latency can tolerate it, or route to a lower-cost background pool for noncritical calls.
[02:52] Priya: what about quantization? you said you tried 4-bit quantize?
[02:56] Marco: we used q4_0-ish profile; model size dropped ~45% and throughput improved ~15% in our tests relative to int8 path because kernel selection favors that representation on our runtime. That also reduces GPU memory pressure so you can fit more instances per card. Cost per effective token improved ~12%. There's occasional slight quality delta on few edge-case prompts — we flagged those in the eval sheet.
[03:18] Tom: any concerns about deterministic outputs after quantization for our A/B tests?
[03:22] Marco: we include a regression alert pipeline; so if we see drift beyond threshold we can pin to the float baseline for those routes. The rollback is simple.
[03:30] Sarah: back to numbers — can you show combined effect? if we do caching + q4 + batch 4 what's tokens/sec/$ roughly?
[03:37] Marco: rough math: baseline 150 tokens/sec/$; quantization +12% -> ~168; caching reduces generation tokens 28% effective, so cost per effective token lowers proportionally — so you'd see effective tokens/sec/$ on served tokens around 168 / (1 - 0.28) ??? oh sorry flipped — simpler: your generation work drops to 72% so dollars spent drop to 0.72x -> tokens/sec/$ increases to 168 / 0.72 ≈ 233 tokens/sec/$. These are approximate and depend on hit-rate and batch distribution.
[04:08] Priya: that 233 tokens/sec/$ would meet our internal target if p95 can be kept under 300ms.
[04:14] Lena: good sign. We'll need to validate under our real traffic shape. Marco, can you run the 100k-req bench with the q4 profile and cache enabled using the sample prompt set Priya gives?
[04:22] Marco: yep I can. I'll produce the traces with latency buckets and batch distributions.
[04:26] Priya: and please include cold-start cases where cache doesn't help so we can see tails.
[04:30] Marco: will do.
[04:32] Tom: operational question — how does Redwood charge on hosted vs dedicated? For budgeting the unit economics differ.
[04:38] Lena: hosted is per-token billing at current public rates; dedicated is a flat node hourly plus lower per-token accounting in our internal model. For high steady throughput dedicated tends to win. For spiky web traffic hosted can be cheaper depending on patterns due to autoscaling. We'll send a side-by-side in the spreadsheet.
[04:53] Tom: any additional infra lock-in or network considerations for private VPC? we may want private early.
[04:58] Marco: private/VPC doesn't change the kernel behavior, just the network and control plane. You still get the same caching/batching runtime features. There are extra ops steps for KMS integration and VPC peering but we documented them.
[05:10] Sarah: what's the expected timeline if we move from pilot to dedicated?
[05:14] Lena: our standard ramp is 2-4 weeks for prod readiness once terms are agreed: capacity sizing, security reviews, and we run a final performance validation.
[05:21] Priya: ok, let's talk about the benchmark configuration — we want 70% web-ish short prompts, 30% long completions, 100k total, with 15% repeats to simulate cache.
[05:30] Marco: perfect. We'll use the profiles and seed traffic shape you described. Also we'll output per-route cost and a tokens/sec/$ breakdown.
[05:36] David: one quick callout — our analytics team needs per-token attribution to product IDs. Can Redwood provide per-request metadata in logs?
[05:43] Marco: yes, we can inject route tags and request metadata into audit logs; sensitive fields can be redacted. We'll add an example log export.
[05:50] Lena: ok. quick recap and next steps before we close?
[05:54] Priya: yes summarize please.
[05:56] Lena: items: Marco run 100k bench with q4 + cache, include cold starts and latency buckets — due 2025-06-11; Marco share batch/trace logs earlier — due 2025-06-05; Lena send updated cost model spreadsheet with hosted vs dedicated scenarios — due 2025-06-06; Priya to share 10k sample prompts by 2025-06-06.
[06:15] Sarah: also re-confirm we'll have another sync 2025-06-11, same time.
[06:19] Tom: thanks all.
[06:21] Lena: great, thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the doc and Slack.
[06:25] Priya: thanks. bye.

Notes: transcript has light transcription noise — some acronyms appear as "KV cash" in the auto notes, model names occasionally hyphenated. References: shared cost spreadsheet (link: drive.google.com/greencart-redwood-costs), benchmark plan doc (link: drive.google.com/gc-poc-bench).
